q: A toddler goes to great lengths to open a box. She knows there is nothing in the box. This is an example of:
who: Intrinsic motivation; compare Harlow's puzzle-solving monkeys

concept.t: Intrinsic motivation means doing something for its own sake: the activity itself is the reward.
The box is empty, so the only reward is the activity of opening it. Compare Harlow's puzzle-solving monkeys, which worked at puzzles with no food on offer.

wrong.b: Would need a bodily imbalance to correct; opening an empty box corrects none.
wrong.c: Needs a separable payoff such as a sweet or praise; the empty box offers none.
wrong.d: Refers to learned social motives such as achievement or approval, none of which is being served here.

q: The phenomenon of "gregariousness" has a:

concept.t: Gregariousness is the tendency to seek the company of others.
It is classed with affiliation among the social (secondary or psychosocial) motives.

wrong.b: Tempts only because McDougall listed gregariousness among his instincts; the classification of motives puts it with the social motives.
wrong.c: Not a standard class name in the classification of motives.
wrong.d: Not a standard class name in the classification of motives either.

q: Which model asserts that inner forces largely beyond individual control drive human behavior?

concept.t: Freud's model places the causes of behaviour in unconscious instincts and conflicts.
The person neither sees nor controls these forces, which is exactly "inner forces largely beyond individual control".

wrong.a: Locates the causes of behaviour in conscious thoughts and beliefs, not hidden forces.
wrong.b: Locates the causes in conditioning and reinforcement from the environment, outside forces rather than inner ones.
wrong.c: Stresses free will and personal growth, the opposite of control by hidden forces.

q: According to Freud, human beings are motivated by powerful 'innate forces' which are known as:

concept.t: Freud's word Trieb is conventionally translated "instinct".
He grouped the instincts into the life instincts (Eros) and the death instinct.

wrong.a: The vocabulary of Maslow and Murray, not Freud.
wrong.b: Hull's term; a fair literal translation of Trieb, but not the classical answer.
wrong.d: The reservoir that holds the instincts, not the forces themselves.

q: Deviations from homeostasis can create an internal state of biological and psychological tension. What is the best term for this state?

concept.t: In Hull's theory a departure from homeostasis is a need, and the aroused, tense state it produces is a drive.
The drive energises behaviour until the need is reduced.

wrong.a: The corrective process (negative feedback), not the tension itself.
wrong.c: Festinger's tension between inconsistent cognitions, not a bodily deviation.
wrong.d: The balanced state that homeostasis restores, the opposite of tension.

q: The Yerkes-Dodson law states that between performance and anxiety, there is:

concept.t: Performance rises with arousal up to a moderate level and then falls, tracing an inverted U (Figure 10.2).
The peak comes at a lower level of arousal for complex tasks.

wrong.b: True but less specific: an inverted U is one kind of curvilinear relationship, so the precise option wins.
wrong.c: Would mean that more anxiety always helps or always hurts, which the law denies.
wrong.d: No two-peaked (M-shaped) version of the law exists.

q: According to Zajonc's drive theory of social facilitation, the presence of others raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response. This means an audience will MOST improve performance on a task that is:
who: Zajonc, drive theory of social facilitation

concept.t: The dominant response is the most probable one; an audience raises arousal, which strengthens it.
On an easy or well-practised task the dominant response is the correct one, so the audience improves performance.

wrong.a: On novel, difficult tasks the dominant response is more often an error, so an audience tends to impair performance.
wrong.c: Here the dominant response is the obvious, stereotyped idea, so an audience tends to impair performance.
wrong.d: On first-time tasks the dominant response is more often an error, so an audience tends to impair performance.

q: In Incentive Theory, motivation is primarily driven by:

concept.t: Incentive theory says behaviour is pulled by external goals, not pushed from within.
Tinklepaugh's lettuce-refusing monkeys and Crespi's contrast effects showed that the goal on offer shapes behaviour.

The same paper asked what drive theory explains motivation as a process to do: reduce physiological needs, not seek external rewards (incentive theory), set long-term goals (goal-setting theory) or increase social connections (affiliation).

wrong.a: The core of self-determination theory, not incentive theory.
wrong.c: Push from within in Hull's theory, whereas incentives pull from outside.
wrong.d: Belong to Bandura's social cognitive theory.

q: Which stage is characterised by realising your full potential according to Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs?

concept.t: Self-actualisation, the top of the hierarchy, is the need to become everything one is capable of becoming.
The lower deficiency needs must be largely met before self-actualisation takes charge.

wrong.a: Concern security and order; a deficiency need that must be largely met first.
wrong.b: Concern belonging and love; a deficiency need that must be largely met first.
wrong.c: Concern respect and achievement; a deficiency need that must be largely met first.

q: According to Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, which need must be mostly fulfilled before an individual seeks esteem needs?

concept.t: The level immediately below esteem is belongingness and love, so it is the need that must be mostly fulfilled just before esteem needs take over.
The printed key gives (b). Physiological needs must be met too, but they come earlier in the sequence (see the Exam trap in Section 10.5).

wrong.a: Lies above esteem, so it cannot be its precondition.
wrong.b: The printed key; must be met as well, but comes earlier in the sequence, so not the best answer to "before esteem".
wrong.d: Must be met as well, but comes earlier in the sequence, so not the best answer to "before esteem".

q: In Reality Therapy, developed by William Glasser, which of the following is considered one of the five basic genetic needs?

concept.t: Glasser's five basic needs are survival, love and belonging, power (achievement and recognition), freedom and fun.
Power or achievement is the only option that appears on Glasser's list.

wrong.a: The top of Maslow's hierarchy (self-actualisation), not a Glasser need.
wrong.c: Jung's inherited layer of the psyche, not a Glasser need.
wrong.d: One of Rogers's therapeutic conditions, not a Glasser need.

q: Viktor Frankl's concept of the "will to meaning," the fundamental motivational force in humans to find purpose in life, is central to which therapeutic school?

concept.t: Frankl held that the primary human motive is the will to meaning, in contrast to Freud's will to pleasure and Adler's will to power.
He built logotherapy on it.

wrong.a: Albert Ellis's therapy, which disputes irrational beliefs.
wrong.c: The school of Rollo May and James Bugental; shares the concern with meaning but is not Frankl's school.
wrong.d: Steven Hayes's therapy, which trains acceptance and values-based action.

q: McClelland's theory of needs proposes three acquired needs that drive behaviour. They are the needs for:

concept.t: McClelland scored achievement, affiliation and power imagery in TAT stories.
He insisted that these needs are learned (acquired), not innate.

wrong.b: Three of Maslow's levels of the hierarchy of needs.
wrong.d: The three innate needs of Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory, not McClelland's acquired ones.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three fundamental psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory?

concept.t: The three innate needs of self-determination theory are autonomy, competence and relatedness.
Affiliation looks like relatedness, which is why it is the bait, but it is McClelland's learned need (nAff), not an SDT need.

The same paper asked which SDT motivation is driven by internal rewards and personal growth: intrinsic motivation, not extrinsic motivation, not amotivation (the absence of motivation) and not external regulation (the least autonomous form of extrinsic motivation).

wrong.a: True: one of the three innate SDT needs, the need to feel that one's actions are self-chosen.
wrong.b: True: one of the three innate SDT needs, the need to feel effective and capable.
wrong.d: True: one of the three innate SDT needs, the need to feel connected to others.

q: Reciprocal causation model has been described under:

concept.t: Bandura's social cognitive theory (1986) rests on triadic reciprocal causation.
Personal factors, behaviour and environment all influence one another.

wrong.b: Names several other theories (Herzberg, Mowrer, Schachter and Singer, Spearman), none of them a reciprocal causation model.
wrong.c: Hull's one-way chain from need to drive to behaviour, not a reciprocal model.
wrong.d: A theory of learning (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner) in which learners actively build their own knowledge, not a causal model of motivation.

q: Social Cognitive Theory highlights the importance of which factor in motivation?

concept.t: Self-efficacy is belief in one's capability to carry out a task.
In Bandura's theory it decides which tasks people attempt, how hard they try and how long they persist.

wrong.a: They do matter in the theory, but not "only"; that word makes it false.
wrong.d: The central variable of Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory.

q: Who introduced the concept of "flow" in psychology?

concept.t: Flow is the absorbed, autotelic state that arises when challenge and skill are in balance.
Csikszentmihalyi described it (1975, 1990).

wrong.a: Rogers described the fully functioning person, not flow.
wrong.b: Maslow's peak experiences are brief, ecstatic moments in self-actualisers, not the flow state.
wrong.d: Frankl described the will to meaning.

q: Arvind is a college student who has strong negative feelings about smoking cigarettes. His grandfather died of lung cancer and he believes smoking is disgusting. One night at a party, Arvind's friends all go outside for a cigarette and he decides to smoke as well. What will he most likely experience as a result?

concept.t: Acting against a strongly held belief creates the tension Festinger (1957) called cognitive dissonance.
Arvind will be motivated to reduce it, perhaps by telling himself that one cigarette at a party does not count.

wrong.a: A particular kind of dissonance reduction after suffering for a goal; Arvind has not suffered for anything.
wrong.b: Nothing in the story suggests an increased drive to smoke; the result is tension, not craving.
wrong.d: Hull's account of satisfying a bodily need; no bodily need is involved here.

q: If Ramesh works in a call centre, and has to work very hard, do a lot of work, and that too at a fast rate, he experiences:
who: Definition of pressure as a stressor

concept.t: Pressure is the demand to perform at a high level, quickly and well (or to conform to others' expectations).
Ramesh's problem is simply the demand itself: hard, heavy, fast work.

wrong.a: Would mean that incompatible motives pull him in different directions.
wrong.b: Would mean that a goal is blocked; nothing blocks Ramesh's goal.
wrong.c: Would mean that he cannot foresee what will happen.

q: The 'satiety centre' of the brain is located in the:

concept.t: Bilateral VMH lesions produce hyperphagia and obesity (Hetherington and Ranson, 1940).
So Stellar's dual-centre theory (1954) called the VMH the satiety centre.
JEMAS 2025 asked the same question with the cerebrum and the basal ganglia as baits; neither is a hunger centre.

wrong.a: The opposite, the feeding centre, whose destruction causes aphagia (Anand and Brobeck, 1951).
wrong.b: Invented by changing one word: hippocampus for hypothalamus.
wrong.c: Invented by changing one word: thalamus for hypothalamus.

q: Masters and Johnson's sexual response cycle is distinct from Kaplan's model. Which of the following correctly reflects Masters and Johnson's sequence?

concept.t: Masters and Johnson (1966) observed four phases in this order: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution.
Helen Singer Kaplan added desire (desire, excitement, orgasm, 1979).

wrong.c: Inserts desire, Kaplan's addition, and ends with "refractory", the male recovery period after orgasm, not a phase of the cycle.
wrong.d: Inserts desire, which is Kaplan's addition, not a Masters and Johnson phase.

q: According to Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which of the following factors are considered motivators that lead to job satisfaction?

concept.t: Herzberg's motivators belong to the content of the work: achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement and growth.
When hygiene factors are poor they cause dissatisfaction, but improving them only removes the dissatisfaction without creating motivation.

wrong.a: Hygiene factors: improving them only removes dissatisfaction, without creating motivation.
wrong.b: Hygiene factors (job security, working conditions): poor ones cause dissatisfaction, good ones do not motivate.
wrong.d: Hygiene factors too: poor ones cause dissatisfaction, good ones do not motivate.

q: Job satisfaction depends on

concept.t: Herzberg's research showed that satisfaction comes from the content of the work (motivators) while dissatisfaction comes from its context (hygiene factors).
So the two together determine how a person feels about the job.

wrong.a: "Or" makes a single source sufficient, but both are needed.
wrong.b: "Only" makes a single source sufficient and leaves out the job environment.
wrong.c: Personal disposition plays a part but is not the only determinant.

q: In Expectancy Theory, motivation is highest when an individual believes: (1) effort leads to performance, (2) performance leads to outcomes, and (3) outcomes are:

concept.t: Vroom's motivational force is expectancy × instrumentality × valence.
The third term, valence, is the value of the outcome to the person.

A second item in the same paper turned the idea round: motivation is highest when effort leads to performance and performance to desired rewards, not when rewards are guaranteed regardless of performance (instrumentality collapses), when effort is unrelated to performance (expectancy is zero) or when rewards are unimportant (valence is zero).

wrong.a: Lowers instrumentality, so motivation falls rather than peaks.
wrong.c: Describes the task rather than the outcome.
wrong.d: A negative valence repels rather than motivates.

q: In Goal-Setting Theory, what characteristic makes a goal most effective at motivating behavior?

concept.t: Locke and Latham found that specific, difficult but attainable goals produce higher performance than vague "do your best" goals or easy goals.
The goals must be accepted by the person (commitment) and accompanied by feedback.
A parallel item in the same paper offered "unrelated to personal values" as a bait; a goal the person does not value wins little commitment, and commitment is another of the theory's conditions.

wrong.a: Vague "do your best" goals produce lower performance than specific ones.
wrong.c: Easy goals produce lower performance than difficult but attainable ones.
wrong.d: Wrong because feedback is one of the conditions that makes goals work.
